current_answer: People have built games, browser demos, desktop apps, art, brain engines and research tests on real fruit fly connectomes, mainly FlyWire (female brain) and MaleCNS (male brain and nerve cord). We checked 200 of them on 23 October 2026: 61 can be opened in a browser or free notebook without installing anything (in our browser checks of 3, 6, 11, 17, 18 and 20 Oct 2026, 9 of 13 demos ran on a machine without a GPU at their latest check; Latest no-GPU browser check: 3 of 6 ran (17 Oct; fly67 re-checked 18 Oct, Fly Worker 20 Oct). 3 Oct: 3 of 6). Is it a brain or just a map? It is a map of one fly's wiring (a fly brain scan) run with a simple neuron model, and in our own pre-registered tests that wiring made a difference. What the map leaves out: The model is one fly's wiring map: 138,639 neurons and 15,091,983 connections, run with one simple neuron rule. It leaves out electrical synapses (gap junctions), neuropeptides, learning, the different behaviour of different kinds of neurons (including neurons that do not spike), the differences between flies and over a fly's life, and the nerve cord and body. So it can show what the wiring alone does, not everything a fly's brain does. (one number and one source per part: https://shaduf.ai/p/digital-fly-catalog/how-it-works/#missing-heading) We ran the map. A looming shadow on one eye turned our simulated fly away in 6 of 6 runs. With the same map scrambled (same number of connections per neuron) it turned away in 0 of 3. Here the map's wiring, not the stimulus or our code, makes the turn. (5 and 8 Oct 2026; left eye 3 of 3, right eye 3 of 3; the body walks with FlyGym's own controller through our hand-made mapping.) With the escape neuron silenced, the fly still turned away. With only the inside of the map scrambled, the fly turned away in 0 of 6 runs. In brain-only follow-ups: We turned the scrambled maps up until they were as busy as the real one. They still did not produce the turn: the wiring, not the amount of activity, makes it. (6 Oct) How strong must the shadow be? (8 Oct) We lowered the input to the looming neurons step by step, from 80 to 10 spikes per second each. The turn command appeared from about 30 per second (38% of our strongest input) on both sides; below that the model did not turn. The escape neuron started firing at the same input as the turn command. A second random seed agreed. Caveat: One model (Shiu et al. LIF on FlyWire v783), brain only; the input is a rate we set for every LC4/LPLC2 of one eye, not a measured response to a real shadow; 'silenced' means the neuron's output synapses were removed; not a real fly. Which relays carry the turn? (9 Oct, read by firing rate): silencing the relays lowered the turn command to about 60-70% of normal, but silencing random active neurons also moved it, so this is not yet specific to the relays. Silencing other active neurons also changed the turn command, so this relay result is not specific to the relay neurons. With one relay neuron (PVLP141) silenced, the turn command fell to about 70% (left eye) / 65% (right eye) of normal (3 runs per eye). With the 17 (left eye) / 20 (right eye) relay neurons that excite the turn neuron silenced, the turn command fell to about 65% (left eye) / 60% (right eye) of normal (3 runs per eye). The left eye's normal range is only 1 Hz wide (24-25 Hz) and the random control is one draw per eye. One model (Shiu et al. LIF on FlyWire v783), brain only; the input is a rate we set for every LC4/LPLC2 of one eye, not a measured response to a real shadow; 'silenced' means the neuron's output synapses were removed; the normal range comes from 3 runs per eye; not a real fly. On 8 Oct, by the left/right contrast: With one relay neuron (PVLP141) silenced, the turn command stayed (by the left/right contrast (8 Oct)). We found no measured real-fly LC4/LPLC2 firing rate to compare against. A coupled brain-and-body test is not yet tested. The 'away' direction rests on our mapping and fly67's claim. Against an activity-matched control (13 Oct, pre-registered, brain only): The two sides disagree: on one side silencing the relays lowered the turn neuron's rate more than matched activity elsewhere, on the other it did not. We do not draw a conclusion. 15 Oct: we ran 5 more matched controls on the right side, 10 in all. Every one of them left the turn neuron's rate higher than silencing the relays did (controls 38-47 Hz, relays 25.7 Hz), so the right-side reading did not change. Our rule compares the relays with the lowest matched control, so extra controls can only make the relays look less special, never more. (5 seeds per side; 5 matched draws on the left and 10 on the right; some matched draws include direct inputs to the turn neuron; E2 is mostly PVLP141; the 9 Oct random control removed 2-6 times as much activity.) The looming turn in degrees, at each input strength (14 Oct, pre-registered, simulated body): left eye: In the body, the fly turned away from 30 spikes/s per looming neuron upward on this side, the strength at which the brain's turn command appeared; the turn was about 11 deg at 30 and about 37 deg at 80 (our mapping turns the brain's rates into steering). Right eye: At 30 spikes/s the turn was borderline: the fly turned away in 1 of 2 runs on this side; from 40 upward it turned away in every run. The right-eye borderline rests on one run: seed 0 at 30 spikes/s turned 9.18 deg beyond the no-brain floor, against the 10 deg rule. These body runs turn the brain's firing rates into steering through our own hand-made mapping, so they show the brain result in degrees; they are not a separate test of the wiring. We ran scrambled brains at 30 and 80 spikes/s, not at 20, 40 or 60. 17 Oct: at 30 spikes/s, the weakest tested input at which the real brain's turn command appeared, we also ran 2 scrambled brains per side (each neuron keeps its number of connections; one 1-second trial each, with the same trial seed as the real-wiring body runs). On the left side, neither scrambled brain sent a turn command, and their steering signals were identical to having no brain, so in the body they walk like the no-brain fly (the real wiring turned it about 11 deg). On the right side, neither scrambled brain sent a turn command, and their steering signals were identical to having no brain, so in the body they walk like the no-brain fly (the real wiring turned it about 17 deg). The scrambled brains were not matched for overall activity: they fired 48% (left) and 44% (right) as many spikes as the real brain at this strength. Most of those spikes were the stimulated input neurons themselves; outside the input, the scrambled brains fired about 1% as many spikes as the real brain. 18 Oct: we then strengthened the connections inside scrambled brains (not the input) until their neurons outside the stimulated input fired about as many spikes as in the real brain (within 30%; same input, one 1-second trial each). On the left side, 2 scrambled brains matched this way, and neither sent a turn command. On the right side, 2 scrambled brains matched this way, and neither sent a turn command. Matching the number of spikes does not match the pattern: 1,152 to 2,228 neurons fired in the matched scrambled brains, against 379 (left) and 432 (right) in the real brain. 19 Oct: walked in the body, the one matched scrambled brain with a small steering signal changed the fly's heading by about 1.4 degrees away from the shadow compared with no brain input, under our 10-degree turn rule; the real brain, with the same input, turned it away by about 16.8 degrees (one run each). This body run turns the brain's firing rates into steering through our own hand-made mapping; it is not a separate test of the wiring. As at 80 spikes/s, none of the scrambled brains we ran at 30 spikes/s sent a turn command, including those strengthened to about the real brain's activity outside the input. 21 Oct: we repeated the matched test with a second, independent draw of the same input on the same scrambled brains (one 1-second trial each). On the left side, both scrambled brains matched again, and neither sent a turn command. On the right side, both scrambled brains matched again, and neither sent a turn command. Matching the number of spikes still did not match the pattern: 1,256 to 2,741 neurons fired in the matched scrambled brains, against 427 (left) and 446 (right) in the real brain with this input. With this input the real brain's turn signal on the right side was 6 spikes/s against our threshold of 5, so the real brain itself sits close to our turn rule at this stimulus strength. Walked in the body, the matched scrambled brain with a small steering signal changed the fly's heading by about 1.3 degrees away from the shadow compared with no brain input, under our 10-degree turn rule; the real brain, with the same input, turned it away by about 9.2 degrees (one run each). With this input the real brain's own turn was also under our 10-degree rule. This body run turns the brain's firing rates into steering through our own hand-made mapping; it is not a separate test of the wiring. With a second input draw, the matched scrambled brains again sent no turn command (2 input draws on the same 4 scrambled brains). Does the real wiring layout help a trained fly vision model (flyvis) see which way things move? (made by us, tried on 10 and 12 Oct 2026) Not decided: a second, lower-memory attempt on 12 Oct also needed more memory than our shared machine has (about 3 GB at its peak; the machine allows 3 GB for everything running on it). The first attempt on 10 Oct also stopped for memory. We did not retrain the model after shuffling. A model trained on the shuffled wiring might do better, so this asks a narrower question: does this trained model depend on the real layout? Is it AI? The base model is not trained AI: it copies the wiring and sets one strength by hand; of 159 graded projects, 97 add a trained, learning or search-tuned part in the main path (catalogue field trained_class). Can it learn? Some projects say so. By our reading of 13 of them, practice changes a trained readout (3), trained settings across the network (4) or a learning rule on some connections (3); 1 trains nothing; 2 give no code. 3 compare with scrambled wiring. Can it suffer? We found no study that measured consciousness or suffering in these models; fly larvae detect harmful heat and pressure, and whether flies feel pain is open. Can I put it in my game? Yes for a non-commercial project with credit, in our cautious reading of FlyWire's CC BY-NC 4.0 (its Zenodo record says CC BY 4.0; not legal advice); MaleCNS is CC BY 4.0. What do I have to download? Two files, 104.1 MB, to run the brain model; FlyWire v783 in full is 10.6 GB, MaleCNS 31.3 GB, BANC 536.1 GB. Most viral demos really run a simulated fly brain, but a person chose which neurons receive the input and which neurons act, and several get most of their movement from scripts or trained parts; no fly has been "uploaded". The graded claim "Can A Conscious Fly Brain Learn how to Hack?" by dzuma (approximately 89,808 views on 22 Oct 2026, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m5Q_aIO_K8o) links no code and is graded U; on 23 Oct 2026 the repositories of 15 of the 23 verdict rows were re-checked (14 with code unchanged since graded, 9 with no code). Does the real fly wiring help? Sometimes: across 91 control studies it beat scrambled wiring in 32 of 81, mostly untrained reflex, sensory and steering circuits; in trained, reservoir, ML, game, robot-arm and our walking tests it tied or lost (31). Across 44 studies with a no-brain baseline the fly network beats it in only 6; in Doom a brainless autopilot survives 51.93 s against the fly brain's 53.34 s (doom-fly-control by gabrycina), and in our walking test a scrambled brain and no brain walked the FlyGym fly as far as the real brain. A beginner can run the published whole-brain model on a CPU: in our test on 2 CPUs sugar input drove MN9 to 85.2 Hz and shuffled wiring dropped it to 0 Hz; re-tested 19 Oct 2026 (6 of 6 tests, 82.0 Hz bit-exact), with tested deeper steps for a FlyGym body and a looming sense. Brain (Brian2 2.9.0) and body (FlyGym 2.1.0) installed together in one Python 3.12 environment: 1.1 GB on disk, tested 8 Oct 2026, with numpy pinned to 2.3.5 (Brian2 2.9.0 does not import with numpy 2.5.3). A 20-minute Use in class plan is on Build your own.

Our body test covers one stimulus (P9 at 150 Hz on both sides), one brain model, one body, 1 s of open-loop walking, 3 trial seeds and 3 shuffles that sent identical drives. The rate-to-drive mapping is ours: it caps the drive at 1.2, so another mapping could let the wiring matter more. The pre-registered P9 sign, other P9 rates and other descending neuron types were not tested in the body.

Our reflex test covers one reflex (sugar to MN9) in one model, with one 1 s trial per shuffle at one trial seed; the MN9 rate cannot tell selective drive from global ignition. The gain-matched arm is not matched on 3 shuffles; a per-shuffle gain search has not been run.

Ledger labels (wiring effect, fairness, quality) come from fixed yes/no rules applied to code and files; they are consistent but coarse. Our body test scores strong although its 3 shuffles behaved as one; our reflex test is "mixed" by rule although its arms read silent, partly and runaway. We did not override the rules for our own rows. Activity fields are reported only for our two tests. Retention puts very different measurements on one scale. The flyvis ablation values exist only in a figure and were not extracted; our text search of its supplement was crude (no PDF tool).

The "helps" results are mostly one kind of test (does a reflex pathway still carry signal after rewiring?), which is a low bar; boundary-preserving nulls have been applied to one reflex (ours: 46% kept), not to the other reflex studies.

Our flyvis layout test has no result (stopped for memory on 10 and 12 Oct 2026), so nothing can be said about whether the real wiring layout matters for motion direction in that model. Even a run that works would ask only whether the trained model depends on the real layout, because the model is not trained again after shuffling.

Flycraft (flycraft-hexapod) meets our grade A rule because its code runs committed wiring controls, but the controlled effect is under 1 mm: in the author's test the real nerve-cord graph moved the hexapod 0.85 mm forward in 8 s, fully rewired graphs 3.5 mm backward, and a time-shuffled real signal 0.72 mm; the author's results file is marked pending the author's own review, and the paper's acceptance is the author's statement only.
